title: Guidelines for Ensuring the Proper Development and Use of AI-Related Technologies (Provisional Translation)

covered_actors: Utilization business operators (including overseas business operators, AI-based system operators, and service providers)

evidence.quote: Identifying and evaluating the risks posed by AI, and implementing appropriate measures according to the potential impact based on the ﬁelds and purposes for which AI is utilized

including organizational processes for identifying, assessing, and addressing risks throughout the entire AI lifecycle (design, development, provision, implementation, etc.), such as mechanisms for monitoring and evaluation involving management

It is desirable to adopt diverse internal testing methods and independent external testing methods by combining various techniques such as red teaming, and to implement appropriate measures to address identiﬁed risks and vulnerabilities.
The scope and conditions for utilizing AI should be subject to a ﬁnal decision made by a human
Appropriately ensuring transparency by disclosing information and securing post-hoc veriﬁability within the limits of what is necessary and technically feasible, to enhance reliability in AI

Furthermore, when providing AI, supplying users with information enabling its proper use (such as the AI's mechanisms and limitations, prohibited actions, data collection policies for training, and warnings regarding output reliability18).

Ensuring explainability within reasonable limits to building trust with stakeholders17 regarding the origin of training data and generated outputs, including the appropriate implementation of intellectual property and privacy protections.

To ensure appropriate transparency of training data, R&D institutes and utilization business operators will display the information (such as websites) used as the basis for AI outputs. When disclosure of training data is requested, it is desirable to respond as much as possible.

R&D institutes and utilization business operators will strive to develop technologies that can determine whether something is generated by AI (digital watermarks, provenance management, APIs19, etc.) and will implement them as necessary.

This guideline, based on Article 13 of the Act on Promotion of Research & Development(R&D), and Utilization of Artiﬁcial Intelligence-Related Technology (AI Act, Act No. 53 of 2025), is formulated in accordance with international norms toward realization of trustworthy AI, aiming to encourage voluntary and proactive eﬀorts by all stakeholders

under the expectation that each stakeholder will voluntarily advance its own initiatives based on the characteristics, intended uses, and purpose of the AI it researches, develops and utilizes, as well as its position and social role

policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Formulated under Article 13 of Japan's AI Act (Act No. 53 of 2025) as a provisional English translation of the December 19, 2025 decision. The guideline encourages voluntary, risk-based, agile lifecycle AI governance aligned with the Hiroshima AI Process and international standards (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001), explicitly encompasses overseas utilization business operators, directs national ministries/agencies to appoint AI governance officers (referencing Chief AI Officers) and local governments to designate responsible officers, and commits the government to continuously review and revise domestic AI guidelines.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: Innovation enablement is the dominant frame because the guideline, issued under Japan's AI Promotion Act, explicitly rejects rigid single standards in favor of voluntary, agile, risk-based governance designed to promote social implementation, lower adoption barriers, foster high-quality data ecosystems, and maximize AI benefits through leading public-sector utilization. Fundamental rights is the strongest runner-up—anchoring the guideline's core 'human-centricity' principles in human dignity, fundamental human rights, fairness/non-discrimination, and privacy—but these principles are consistently framed as guardrails that enable trustworthy adoption and innovation rather than as the sole overarching mandate. Consumer and public safety (preventing physical harm, fraud, crime, deepfake abuse, and system failures) and social stability (containing misinformation and disinformation) form substantial secondary rationales, alongside economic competitiveness (growth, fair competition, corporate advantage, and global leadership via the Hiroshima AI Process), while national security and labor transition appear only briefly in risk lists and skills guidance.

evidence_spans.quote: AI contributes to economic growth and the advancement of peopleʼs lives and it is important to promote its social implementation and innovation.

Furthermore, to reduce barriers to AI adoption in various contexts, with regard to issues that can be anticipated or that may arise when utilizing AI, the government will organize the issues and ideas regarding the interpretation and application of where responsibility lies, and strive to clarify interpretations as much as possible based on precedents, etc.
Respecting human dignity and fundamental human rights, and complying with the laws and regulations
Identifying and evaluating the risks of illegal activities such as various crimes including cyberattacks and fraud perpetrated through the misuse of AI, and implementing appropriate measures.

In particular, given that the spread of misinformation and disinformation generated by AI poses a serious risk, R&D institutes and utilization business operators will strive to develop technologies that can determine whether something is generated by AI (digital watermarks, provenance management, APIs19, etc.) and will implement them as necessary.
Proactively disclosing and explaining these initiatives is expected to enhance corporate value and secure competitive advantage.
